newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks try to stay above 19,000 in week ahead.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks try to stay above 19,000 in week ahead.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market's key index is likely to struggle to find a firm foothold at the 19,000 level this week, after it ended above that threshold on Friday for the first time this year.

"The benchmark has reached a stage where it is getting close to retracing one-third of its worth from the January 10 low of 17,303 and the high of 22,666 marked on June 26," Okasan Securities general manager Akihiro Naemura said.
"Consolidation at the one-third retracement level is needed before further rises can be achieved," he added.
On Friday, the Nikkei average of 225 leading shares, studded with global blue-chips, ended down 17.17 points or 0.09 percent at 19,034.54. In the course of the week, the barometer rose 312.54 points.

The Nikkei average's return to the 19,000 level was ignited by newspaper reports on Thursday that the government may use public funds to buy land formerly owned by failed housing loan firms and other troubled financial institutions.
Banking, construction and real estate -- sectors groaning under the weight of problem loans which were punished by fierce selling in recent months -- were bought back.

Media reports on Friday that the government may ease regulations on floor-area ratios in new buildings in cities to increase the number of high-rise apartment blocks also lent support to property-related shares, said Yasuo Ueki, Nikko Securities general manager.

The TOPIX index, encompassing most of the banking, construction and other sectors saddled with bad loans, finished with modest gains on Friday. It rose 13.35 points or 0.95 percent to end at 1,425.01 on hopes that help was on the way for the troubled sectors.

In contrast with the interest in domestic issues, the return of the yen to the level of 122 to the dollar from 124 earlier in the week nourished profit-taking of recently high flying, export-strong blue-chip issues, brokers said.

"Before, it was global issues which were being bought and problem loan-related issues being sold, but the tables have turned," said Yamaichi Securities deputy general manager Hisao Suzuki. Further strengthening of the yen could fuel profit-taking of exporters, and if buying of domestic issues and blue-chips peters out, market sentiment could sour, a broker at a second-tier brokerage said.
He added, however, that it was unlikely that the Nikkei average would sink below the January 10 low.
Market sources expect the Nikkei average to rove between 18,500 and 19,700 in the coming week.
